q: The front portion of the eye is covered by a tough, transparent membrane called the _____.
e: The cornea is the tough transparent front membrane of the eye. Opaque would block the image at the door. The cornea is the front window; the retina is the back screen.

q: The region between the cornea and the eyelens is filled with a transparent liquid called the _____ humour.
e: The cornea is the tough transparent front membrane of the eye. Opaque would block the image at the door. The front chamber holds aqueous humour, not a saline label.

q: The region between the eyelens and the retina contains a transparent liquid called the _____ humour.
e: The retina is the light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye, with rods and cones. The image there is real, inverted and smaller than the object. Vitreous humour is in the eye, not cerebrospinal fluid.

q: The _____ is the colored portion of the eye which controls the amount of light energy entering the eye.
e: The iris is the coloured part of the eye and controls how much light enters. The pupil is the hole in its centre, the eye's aperture. The iris is the coloured shutter; the pupil is the hole.

q: The pupil automatically _____ in dim light and contracts in bright light.
e: The pupil is the hole in the iris, the eye's aperture. It dilates in dim light and contracts in bright light. In dim light the pupil dilates.

q: The _____ muscles are attached to the eyelens and can vary its thickness to alter the focal length.
e: Ciliary muscles change eyelens thickness and so change focal length. They contract for near vision, making the lens more convex. Ciliary muscles, not skeletal muscles, squeeze the eyelens.

q: When near objects are viewed, the ciliary muscles _____ and permit the eyelens to form a more convex shape.
e: Ciliary muscles attach to the eyelens and change its thickness, hence its focal length. For near objects they contract and the lens becomes more convex. Near vision contracts the ciliary muscle.

q: The retina consists of light-sensitive cells called rods and _____.
e: The retina at the back of the eye holds rods and cones. The yellow spot is cone-packed and most sensitive for fine detail. The retina's cells are rods and cones, not cilia.

q: The _____ spot is the most light-sensitive spot on the retina and consists of cones exclusively.
e: The retina is the light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye, with rods and cones. The image there is real, inverted and smaller than the object. The yellow spot is most sensitive; the blind spot has no receptors.

q: The spot on the retina which has no rods or cones is called the _____ spot.
e: The retina at the back of the eye holds rods and cones. The yellow spot is cone-packed and most sensitive for fine detail. No rods or cones means the blind spot.

q: The image of an object formed on the retina is real, inverted and _____ than the size of the object.
e: The retina is the light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye, with rods and cones. The image there is real, inverted and smaller than the object. The retinal image is smaller than the object.

q: Farsightedness is a defect of vision in which distant objects are seen clearly, but objects nearby are _____.
e: Farsightedness, hyperopia: distant objects are clear, nearby ones are blurry. Near rays meet behind the retina, so a converging convex lens is the correction. Nearby objects in hyperopia look blurry, not invisible.

q: Farsightedness can be corrected by the use of spectacles with a _____ lens.
e: Farsightedness, hyperopia: distant objects are clear, nearby ones are blurry. Near rays meet behind the retina, so a converging convex lens is the correction. A camera and a microscope objective need a convex converging lens.

q: Nearsightedness is caused by an eyeball which is too _____ or due to the eyelens which is more convex than necessary.
e: Nearsightedness, myopia: near objects are clear, distant ones are blurry. Distant rays meet in front of the retina, so a diverging concave lens is the correction. A convex lens would add even more convergence. Nearsightedness is caused by an eyeball which cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Nearsightedness can be corrected by the use of spectacles with a _____ lens.
e: Nearsightedness, myopia: near objects are clear, distant ones are blurry. Distant rays meet in front of the retina, so a diverging concave lens is the correction. A convex lens would add even more convergence. Corrected by the use of spectacles with cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: For normal vision, the least distance of distinct vision is about _____ cm.
e: Least distance of distinct vision is about 25 cm for a normal eye. Nearer than that, the lens cannot bulge enough. The far point for normal vision is infinity. Normal vision the least distance of distinct cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: For normal vision, the maximum distance of distinct vision is _____.
e: A bright maximum needs constructive interference, integer path difference. On a grating, d sin theta = m lambda locates those maxima. Half-integer path difference is a minimum. Normal vision the maximum distance of distinct cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The light energy falling on the retina is transmitted to the brain by the _____ nerve.
e: The retina is the light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye, with rods and cones. The image there is real, inverted and smaller than the object. The optic nerve then carries that signal to the brain. Energy falling on the retina is transmitted cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: In the human eye, the _____ is in the centre of the iris and the light passes through it.
e: The iris is the coloured part of the eye and controls how much light enters. The pupil is the hole in its centre, the eye's aperture. Rainbows off a disc are grating colours.

q: When distant objects are viewed, the ciliary muscles relax and the eyelens becomes _____ convex.
e: Ciliary muscles attach to the eyelens and change its thickness, hence its focal length. For near objects they contract and the lens becomes more convex. For distant objects they relax and the lens flattens. Objects are viewed the ciliary muscles relax cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.
